title: Why Was a 5,500-Year-Old Shoe Still Laced Up?
description: Why was a 5,500-year-old shoe still laced up when archaeologists discovered it in Armenia? Discover how ancient cave conditions and sheep manure preserved the world's oldest leather footwear.
facts_to_check: Areni-1 shoe discovered in 2008 in Armenia by Diana Zardaryan
Radiocarbon dated to approximately 3500 BC (around 5,500 years old)
Dating conducted by Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit and UC Irvine
Preserved by cool dry cave conditions and covered in a layer of sheep dung
Stuffed with grass inside and tied with leather laces through eyelets

scenes.narration: A young researcher reached into a deep crust of dried [[sheep manure]] and pulled out a leather shoe with its laces still tied.
The right-foot slipper was crafted from a single piece of [[yellow cowhide]], custom fitted to a human foot over five thousand years ago.
Inside the cave, archaeologists found ancient wine vats, dried grapes, and obsidian blades, but this [[lonely slipper]] stole the entire show.
Scientists sent small leather samples to laboratories in Oxford and California to figure out just how old this [[footwear]] really was.
Radiocarbon testing confirmed the leather dated back to around [[thirty-five hundred BC]], making it older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.
It was even older than Stonehenge, pre-dating famous icy traveler [[Otzi the Iceman]] by several hundred remarkable historical years.
But how could organic animal hide stay soft and flexible without turning into [[brittle dust]] after thousands of long years?
The secret lay inside the unique environmental conditions of the [[Areni cave]] nestled high in the Armenian mountain wilderness.
Stable temperature, low humidity, and a thick protective carpet of ancient [[goat droppings]] created the ultimate natural sealed storage vault.
The manure locked out oxygen and destructive microbes, preserving the delicate [[tanned hide]] almost exactly as its owner left it.
Researchers also discovered [[dry grass]] stuffed neatly inside the heel and toe, acting like a modern shoe tree to hold its shape.
Some experts believe the grass provided cozy [[winter insulation]], while others think it was placed there to preserve the leather contour.
Threaded through fifteen pairs of neatly punched eyelets was a [[leather thong]], crisscrossed and fastened tight just like modern sneakers today.
Nobody knows if the owner lost it, abandoned it, or left it as a ritual gift to the [[ancient cave]] spirits.
But thanks to a thick blanket of sheep manure, that single [[tied shoelace]] waited five millennia to tell its legendary story.
